sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise originale produite avec l'assistance d'un modele de langage (Claude, Anthropic), a partir du texte grec de zoo71/2g.xml (edition Sbordone 1936, "Redactio secunda quae vocatur Byzantina", pp. 149-256), lui-meme deja present dans le corpus Zoomathia. Traduction generee par IA, non relue par un specialiste : a verifier avant tout usage scientifique cite. 28 chapitres correspondant exactement au decoupage du temoin grec (memes xml:id ; les chapitres 15.1/15.2 et le doublon de numerotation "16" du temoin grec, attribue au chapitre "Concerning the Ant", sont conserves tels quels, sans renumerotation, pour rester fideles a la source).

div.head: Concerning the Lion
div.p: The lion has three natures in himself, after the likeness of the consubstantial Trinity.

The first nature of the lion: when the lioness bears her cub, she bears it dead, and she sits facing it for three days, watching it closely (for if she looks away from it, it does not come to life); and after three days the male lion comes, and breathes into its nostrils the breath of life, and it is quickened and rises up.

So too the unbelieving nations, through the three-day burial and rising of our Lord Jesus Christ, looked up and were quickened; for before baptism they were called dead and blind, though watched over by the lioness, that is, by the Holy Spirit, until the three-day burial. But when the male lion came, that is, the living Word, he breathed into them the Holy Spirit, and quickened them, and raised them all up out of Hades.
The second nature of the lion is this: when it sleeps, its eyes keep watch, and seven paces before the hunter draws near, it knows him beforehand, and flees from him, and is not mastered.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ was in the heavens seated upon his throne, and on earth was crucified by the Jews, and in Hades took the devil captive, and thus fulfils all things threefold in the Monad. For this reason he spoke through the prophet, "I sleep, but my heart waketh."
And the third nature of the lion: when it flees the hunter, it covers its tracks with its tail, and the hunter is not able to track it.
And so you too, understanding man, when you give alms, let not your left hand know what your right hand does, lest the devil track out your good works, and turn you the more toward evil.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the lion.

div.head: Concerning the Hydrops
div.p: The hydrops is a beast greater in size than all other beasts, having in itself two horns shaped like a saw, so as to destroy every animal that comes against it; and it also gnaws at the greatest trees with its horns, and saws through them and cuts them down, and no animal is able to master it. This same hydrops grazes in the eastern land, near the river Ocean, and when it thirsts, it drinks from that river, and is at once made drunk and exults in its soul, and wrestles with the ground, and scrapes the horn of its head upon the earth like an ox worked up by wantonness. There is there a tree called the "tane," having the shape of a vine, with slender shoots and strong branches; and this hydrops, scraping itself and wrestling with the ground, entangles its horns in the branches of the tane and is bound fast. Then the hunter comes, and finds it bound by the horns, and masters it.

And so you too, understanding man, know that God has made you noble beyond the hydrops; and instead of two horns he has given you the two Testaments, that is, the Old and the New, that you might gore the opposing powers, and that nothing evil might come near you; for he said through the prophet David, "Through thee will we push down our enemies, and in thy name we will bring to nought them that rise up against us." The river Ocean is interpreted as the greatness of wealth, and the tane is interpreted as the pleasure of life. Man becomes entangled in the pleasures of life, and neglects the faith, and the hunter comes, that is, the devil, and finds him entangled in life and neglectful of the faith, and masters him.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the hydrops.

div.head: Concerning the Elephant
div.p: The elephant is a beast of great size, having in itself a trunk with which to destroy every animal, [and by which likewise it governs both its eating and its drinking]; and having no joints in itself, it cannot bend down and go to sleep. The male walks together with the female, and as they graze, it happens that the female finds the plant called the mandrake, and partakes of it, and is at once inflamed, and goes to the male, and, sporting with him, offers him a share of the same plant; and the male too tastes it, and is at once inflamed likewise, and unites with the female, and she becomes pregnant. And when the days draw near for the female to give birth, in what manner does she act? She enters into pools of water, and measures the water until it comes up to her udders, and so gives birth (for if she should give birth on dry land, she would not be able to rise up again, having no joints in her knees); and the newborn elephant swims through the waters, and so suckles its mother [for seven days], and when it can walk with its own steps, it comes forth out of the waters [together with its parents]. And when it wishes to sleep, in what manner does it act? It goes to leaning trees, and rests against them, and so sleeps. And in what manner does the hunter catch it? [Knowing such trees, where the elephant sleeps,] the hunter goes beforehand to the place where the elephant grazes, and saws through the tree, nearly all the way through, so as to fell it. Then the elephant comes, not knowing that the tree has been sawn through, and leans against it, wishing to sleep, and at once the tree breaks, and throws it down, and it lies fallen and unable to rise up of itself. Then the hunter comes, and finds it fallen, and takes whatever he needs from that elephant. But if the hunter does not come upon it, in what manner is the same elephant raised up? It cries out with a great voice, [wild] and full of pain, and at its voice a great elephant will come, and coming, will labour, yet will not be able to raise up the one that has fallen; [and it will cry out again, and four will come, and not even these will be able to raise it up;] then the two elephants will cry out, and at their voice twelve elephants will come, and they too, coming, will labour and will not be able to raise up the fallen one; then the twelve elephants together with the other two will cry out, and at their voice a small elephant will come, and it, coming, will put its trunk beneath the fallen one, and will exert its strength beneath it, and by skill and art will raise up the one that has fallen.

Let us begin, then, to unfold this parable: it is plain that it concerns the first-formed Adam and Eve. For just as Eve first tasted of the tree of disobedience and gave to her husband also, so too the female elephant first tasted of the plant, and gave to the male also. And what does it mean that she tasted? That she transgressed. And what does it mean that she conceived? That she sinned. And what is the pool of the birth? Paradise. And what are the leaning trees? The fence of paradise. And who is the one who saws the tree? The devil. And what is the axe? The tongue of the serpent. And what does it mean that it fell? That it was cast out. And who is the great elephant, who was not able to raise it up? The prophet Moses. [And who are the four? The evangelists.] And who are the twelve elephants? The twelve apostles. And who is the small elephant, who raised it up? Christ; for he it was who raised up Adam out of Hades by his skill.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the elephant.

div.head: Concerning the Stag
div.p: The stag has the shape of a wild gazelle, and its horn is threefold, according to its three renewals. It lives fifty years, and thereafter, as a fine runner, it courses through the glens and the woodlands [and the thickets] of the mountains, and it scents out the holes of creeping things; and wherever there is a thrice-sloughed serpent, it perceives it by its keen sense of smell, and at once utters three very great and fierce cries, and sets its snout at the mouth of the hole, and draws in its breath, and however deep the serpent lies, it is drawn up into the stag's throat, and so is swallowed down; for this reason it is called "elaphos" [stag], from its "taking" [helein] serpents out of the depths. And having taken the serpent, it runs to the springs of water; for if within three hours of taking the serpent it does not drink water, it dies, but if it drinks water, it will live another fifty years. For this reason the prophet David said, "As the hart longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for thee, O God."

And so you too, understanding man, have three renewals in yourself, [that is,] the baptism of incorruption, the grace of adoption, and repentance; and when you take the serpent into your heart, that is, sin, run at once to the springs of water, that is, to the veins of the divine Scriptures and the interpretations of prophecy, and drink living water, that is, partake of the holy gifts in repentance; renew yourself henceforth by repentance, and be not dead in sin.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the stag.

div.head: Concerning the Hydrippus
div.p: The hydrippus has the shape of a horse from the middle upward, and from the middle downward it has the shape of a sea-monster. This hydrippus travels in the sea, in the eastern land, [and is the commander of all the fish]; it is fixed upon a rock, and the waves do not destroy it; [and in the region of the eastern land there stands a fish having the colour of gold], and its appearance is as of gold, [and it does not move from its place]. And when the fish of the sea grow inflamed, they go to the hydrippus, [and it, being as it were commander of all the fish, goes toward the eastern land, toward the golden fish, and all the fish go with it, swimming together]; those toward the north swim toward the south, and those toward the south swim toward the north. [And they go toward the golden fish, and the hydrippus, coming near, licks it all over, and all the male fish likewise lick it]; for if they do not go to it and greet it and do it reverence as king of the fish, they do not conceive. [And they go each to their own places]. And when they go toward the hydrippus, the females go before and the males behind, and thereupon the fishermen stretch their nets across their way, and the fish, being in a great heat, fall easily into the nets and are caught by the fishermen; so too the men who are made drunk with the pleasures of life are caught by the opposing powers. But when they turn away from the hydrippus, the males swim before and the females behind, and the males cast forth their seed, and the females follow behind them and take the seed into their mouths, and at once conceive, and [after seven days they give birth; for from the time that] they have conceived, they separate from one another and are no longer caught.

And so you too, understanding man, sail toward the east, that is, toward the Church, and do reverence to the hydrippus, that is, to the Lord God, and be made pregnant of the Holy Spirit, and separate yourself from sin and uncleanness, and you will no longer be caught by the opposing powers. [Let us then set forth this parable concerning human nature: the hydrippus is interpreted as Moses, the first-fruits of prophecy; the sea is interpreted as the world; the fish are interpreted as men; the golden fish is interpreted as the way of right belief. For the prophets go first and are caught by the Holy Spirit, and men, being caught by the teachings of the prophets and following after them, become pregnant with the grace of the Holy Spirit. The fishermen are interpreted as the opposing powers, and the nets as the guides of perdition and of the error of Baal, who did not follow the hydrippus, that is, the law of Moses, but turning aside fell into the nets of the hunting demons, and perished; but those who followed the prophecy, snare and net did not overtake them.]
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the hydrippus.

div.head: Concerning the Griffin
div.p: The griffin is a bird of great size, greater than all the birds of the sky. It stands in the eastern land, at the harbour of the river Ocean, and when the sun rises out of the depths of the waters and sprinkles its rays upon the world, this griffin spreads out its wings, and receives the blazing heat of the sun, so that it may not burn up the inhabited earth; and another griffin travels along with the sun as far as its setting, as it is even written upon its wings: "Go forth, light-giver; give light to the world."

In like manner two griffins travel together with the Godhead also, that is, the archangel Michael and the holy Mother of God, and they receive the blazing heat of the sun, that is, the wrath of God, lest he say to all, "I know you not," and his wrath consume them.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the griffin.

div.head: Concerning the Vulture
div.p: The vulture is a bird more gluttonous than all the birds. It fasts for forty days, and again, when it is found among food, it eats forty pounds, and so makes up for the fast of the forty days.

And so you too, understanding man, having fasted forty days, choosing the life-bearing resurrection of the Lord, do not then fall to gluttony and make up in yourself for the forty days of fasting, [lest you lose your reward].

This same vulture, when food fails it [and it finds nothing to eat], by what means does it perceive food? Listen: it sits upon a jutting rock, looking toward the north, and when a carcass occurs in any place whatever, its right claw is dipped [in the blood of the animal], and at once it knows that food has come to be, and immediately it soars up very high, and for this reason it is called "gyps" [vulture], because it rises up on high from the earth [and transforms itself thither]; and when it has risen to its greatest height, there appears to it another sign, like the vapour of a star, and it goes [as a cloud] before its eyes, guiding it toward the food, [and the vulture follows behind it], and when [it draws near to the food], the sign departs from it, [and the vulture] casts itself down to the earth, and is taken up with the food.
And so you too, understanding man, do not exalt yourself, lest, having abandoned yourself from the height, you fall into ruin, that is, into the mire of licentiousness.

But when the female becomes pregnant and the days draw near for her to give birth, she is tormented in her nest for three days, [drowsing and] unable to bring forth. Then the male vulture goes off toward the eastern land, [near the river Ocean], and there is a very deep ravine there, and he casts himself down into the depth of the ravine, and takes the stone that eases birth, and carries it up [and places it] in his nest, and the female easily gives birth, [and at once takes up the stone again]; but the female will not be released from her pain unless the male carries the stone back again to its own place [in the ravine].

And so you too, understanding man, when you fall into sin, lay it aside in its own place, [in the ravine], that is, in the hollow of Hades, that it may heal you of your unclean pain; for fear sin, the mother of punishment, [and drive it away from you, lest, lingering, it destroy your soul together with your body].
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the vulture.

div.head: Concerning the Eagle
div.p: The eagle is king of the birds, and is called "aetos" [eagle] on account of its great age. It lives a hundred years and grows old, [and its beak also grows, and its eyes become dim so that it cannot see,] and it can no longer hunt; then it rises up on high, and casts itself down against a rock, and breaks its beak, and bathes in a clear pool, and sits upon a jutting rock facing the sun, and when the heat of the sun grows thick upon it, the scales fall from its eyes, and it becomes young again.

And so you too, understanding man, when you have sinned greatly, rise up to the height, that is, to your own conscience, cast yourself down against the rock, that is, against the orthodox faith, break your beak, that is, the thrusting-forth of your sins, bathe in a clear pool, that is, in your own tears, sit upon the rock, [that is, the Church, and be warmed] by the sun, that is, by the Holy Spirit; let the warmth of repentance grow thick upon you, cast off from yourself the scales, that is, your sins, and renew yourself again, [as the Prophet says: "thy youth shall be renewed as the eagle's," through confession and righteousness], and you shall be called righteous before God.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the eagle.

div.head: Concerning the Pelican
div.p: The pelican is a bird more fond of its offspring than all the birds [of the sky, and know moreover that] the male and the female both travel together, and make their young; and [when their young are born,] the male goes off to bring food and nourish them, while the female sits in her nest, [guarding her young,] and cherishes them, and greets them and pecks at them in a kiss; and greeting them and pecking at them, she pierces their sides, and they die. And after three days the male will come, and will find them dead, and will grieve his heart greatly, and, inflamed with grief, [at once] he will peck his own side, [and pierce it,] and blood will come forth from his side, and he will let it drip upon the wounds of the dead chicks, and [at once] they are brought back to life.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ had his side opened with a spear by the Jews, and [at once] there came forth blood and water, and it dripped upon the dead chicks, (that is, upon Adam and Eve, and the rest of the prophets, [and upon all who had died]), and he brought them back to life, [and gave light to the inhabited world], through his three-day burial and resurrection. For this reason he said through the prophet David, "I am become like a pelican of the wilderness."
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the pelican.

div.head: Concerning the Phoenix
div.p: The phoenix is a bird more splendid than even the peacock; for the peacock has the colouring of its wings through green and gold, but the phoenix has it through hyacinth-stones and emeralds and precious stones, and it wears a crown upon its head, and a sphere upon its feet, as though it were a king. This phoenix dwells near India [and Heliopolis], and remains [five hundred years] among the cedars of Lebanon, eating nothing at all, but being nourished by the Holy Spirit; [it dwells alone in Lebanon for five hundred years], and after five hundred years it fills its wings with spices, and when the priest of Heliopolis gives the sign, [at once] the phoenix itself rises up from its own place, and goes to the priest [of Heliopolis], and enters the temple, and sits upon the altar of sacrifice, and fire kindles from its feet, and burns up the altar of sacrifice together with the bird itself, and everything becomes ashes; and on the following day the priest [of Heliopolis] goes to it, and finds it a newborn fledgling, and on the second day he will find it grown into feathers, and on the third day he will find it a bird renewed and made whole [as it was from the beginning], and it greets the priest [of Heliopolis], and, [renewed,] goes back again to its own place.

How then can the foolish Jews disbelieve the three-day resurrection of our Lord [Jesus Christ]? For if this bird is brought to life within three days, how did our Lord Jesus Christ, who has power over both the living and the dead, not raise himself up? -- according to what the Prophet said: "the righteous shall flourish like the phoenix, [and] shall multiply like the cedar in Lebanon."
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the phoenix.

div.head: Concerning the Peacock
div.p: The peacock is a bird exceedingly delightful, beyond all the birds of the sky. This peacock, being beautifully coloured and lovely in its wings, walking about [here and there] beholds itself with delight, and shakes itself and struts and glances about; but when it looks upon its feet, it cries out fiercely, weeping; for its feet are not in keeping with the beauty of its form.

And so you too, understanding man, beholding your commandments and your good deeds, [which God has given you], take delight and rejoice and exult in your soul; but when you look upon your feet, that is, your sins, cry out and weep before God, and hate iniquity, just as the peacock hates its own feet, that you may be shown righteous to the Bridegroom.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the peacock.

div.head: Concerning the Bee
div.p: The bee is longed-for and glorious; for he said through the prophet Ezekiel, "the bee is little among winged things, [yet her works are greatest,] and her fruit is the beginning of sweet things."
Her labour is beyond understanding, and sweeter than all foods.
So too the works of God are beyond the understanding of mortals, and wondrous on high, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, and beyond all created things.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the bee.

div.head: Concerning the Partridge
div.p: The partridge is a bird more prolific than all the birds; and when the male and the female have made their nest, and the female begins to lay her eggs day by day, and when the egg is still moist upon her, the brood of her own womb does not suffice her, but the female runs also to other nests, and steals eggs [from those belonging to others, and goes off] so as to multiply her young. [And in what manner does she carry off the stolen eggs? Listen: she gathers them and places them beneath her wings, and walks upon her feet,] and carries them to her own nest; and the one who laid them comes, and seeks the eggs she has lost; then they bring a case against one another over the stolen eggs. For this reason it is called "perdix" [partridge], because it persists in the lawsuit, and will not give back the eggs which it has plundered from another's nest. [And after the young come forth from the eggs, the chicks begin to walk with her, and when they hear the voice of their true mother who laid the eggs, they fly up at once and are carried off to her, abandoning the one who plundered them from her own nest.]

And so you too, understanding man, when you have done many alms-deeds, let them not suffice you, it is said, but run also to other commandments, and multiply your nest greatly, that is, purify your heart, and stand firm at law against the opposing powers; and just as the partridge holds fast in her own nest, not giving back the eggs which she stole, so you too, understanding man, stand firm in your faith, and do not turn back the eggs which you have stolen from the devil, that is, the commandments of God, and you shall not be mastered by the opposing powers. [Interpretation: and you too, O man, even if you should be seized by the wicked demons and hear the reading of the divine Scriptures, understand that it is the mother of those who are saved, and leave the plunderer, and walk in the fear of God, that you may have eternal life.]
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the partridge.

div.head: Concerning the Stork
div.p: The stork is a bird fond of its own home; from the middle upward it is white in appearance, and from the middle downward it is dark. [This stork never abandons its nest, but, it is said, now the male, now the female keeps watch over it,] and they do not leave it alone.

So too our Lord Jesus Christ, at one time shows the things above to all as God, at another time the things below to men as man, neither forsaking the things of heaven, nor abandoning the things of earth.

Know also that these storks travel both together and make their young, and at once the male goes off and brings food, while the female sits and guards them, and they take turns with one another, and they do not forsake their nest.

And so you too, understanding man, let neither morning nor evening pass without prayer, and you shall not be mastered by the devil. And when this stork brings its young to maturity, they all take wing together in a single hour [and a single day] and a single moment, and go off to another place, and again, in their season, they will come back, restoring their own nests, and making their young, in the same manner as our Lord Jesus Christ was taken up from us, and will come again in his own time, restoring the accursed, according to what the Prophet said, "there the sparrows shall make their nests; the house of the heron leads the way for them."
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the stork.

div.head: Concerning the Turtledove
div.p: The turtledove is a bird fonder of its mate than all the birds [of the sky]. The male and the female travel together, and make their young two at a time, and if it happens that one of them dies, [whether male or female,] at once the one who survives goes into the wilderness, [and sits upon a dry tree, mourning its yoke-fellow,] and will not endure to mate with another, but they keep their single union until the end of their life.

And so you too, understanding man, when you have been filled with iniquities and it seems good to you to repent again, lay aside all wickedness, and do not fall into another defilement, that is, into another sin, but keep your single union and your repentance, that you may find a dwelling at the second coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the turtledove.

div.head: Concerning the Turtledove
div.p: And the turtledove was by nature both chaste and virgin and continent; for this reason also, under the old law, in the temple, they used to offer as gifts doves and turtledoves, the one on account of its great fecundity and simplicity, the other on account of its virginity and continence. And if it should happen that one of the pair dies, it is no longer joined in a second union, but mourns for the rest of its life; for it never rests upon a tree thick with shade, lest its heart flourish, nor does it drink clear water, lest it increase the desire of its heart, but it muddies the water with its wings, and drinks it so, that it may pass its life in chastity.

div.head: Concerning the Dove
div.p: The dove is more glorious than all the birds; know [concerning the white and the fiery-coloured dove] that doves travel white and dappled and [black and] dark and fiery-coloured, and they make their young [in the depths of the towers, and nourish them], and are unable to fly on their own, until the fiery-coloured dove comes running and gives them food, [and only then do they fly].

So too, at the coming of the Saviour, [the prophets] Moses and Aaron, Samuel and David [and Daniel], Micah and Malachi, Isaiah and Jeremiah, and all the rest of the prophets spoke [concerning Jesus], and were not able to confirm the word, until the fiery-coloured dove passed through, that is, John the Baptist, and [more than the others] confirmed the word, showing to all [and saying], "Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world," and he healed our sicknesses.

[Well then has the Physiologus spoken concerning the fiery-coloured dove.] The Physiologus spoke concerning the dove according to the saying, "be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves"; for doves, flying together in close ranks, fly with one accord, and on account of the concord of their wings the swift-winged hawk cannot seize one of them; [but if it finds one alone, it seizes it].

And so you too, understanding man, do not remove yourself far from the Church, lest the enemy find you [naked, that is, without wings, that is to say without virtues, and] alone, and put you to death [unto perdition, that is, the devil].
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the dove.

div.head: Concerning the Asp
div.p: The asp has the shape of a fierce cat. The male keeps to the east, and the female to the west, and when the day of their desire comes, [that they may unite,] the male comes from the east and the female from the west, and they join together at midday; and the female does not, by nature, allow the male to unite with her, but rather opens her mouth, and the male puts his head inside the female, and the female, clenching her teeth, kills the male for the pleasure of her desire, and so conceives, [and behold, the male dies]; and when she is about to give birth, since she has no other means, her offspring gnaw through the belly of their mother and come forth, and their mother dies, [for she has no other nature, and so the mother dies also, and] thereupon they come forth as slayers of both father and mother. [And when their young reach maturity, at once the male runs again to the east and the female to the west, in the same manner as their parents, until the hour of their desire comes again.]

This same asp, wherever it lies in a threshing-floor place, burns the grass of the earth, and by the fierceness of its breath it burns the dust of the earth from three paces away, and from seven paces no one dares to draw near, on account of the fierceness of its poison; and if anyone draws near in that place, from man to beast, he dies. And in what manner does the charmer master it? Listen: he goes to the place where the asp lies, and, [having gone there,] makes seven handfuls of green herbs, and steeps them in water for seven days, until they grow soft, and takes a staff twelve cubits long, and stops up his temples and his ears and his nose, that he may not smell its breath, and goes toward it charming from afar, and, [as he charms,] draws near to it, and casts handfuls of herbs toward it, and its first fierce heat burns them, and its second fierce heat makes them shudder through and through, and the third dries them, and the fourth chills them, and the fifth causes them to drip, and the sixth warms them, and the seventh has no power left. Then, as he draws near charming, the asp sees the charmer coming upon it, and it stops up its ears, that it may not hear his voice and die; for this reason [it stops up its ears together with its tail; for if it should hear his voice, it dies at once], and the Prophet says of it, "like the deaf asp that stops her ears; which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charmed cunningly by a skilled one." And when he draws near to it, he stretches out the staff of twelve cubits, and pulls its tail away from its hearing, and he raises his voice, and the asp hears his voice, and at once dies, and the charmer takes from it whatever he needs.

So too the Jews were troubled in their own time by their own desire and the hardening of their heart, and they consumed the head of the male, that is, the Law and the Prophets, they consumed [the head] of the female, that is, John and the apostles, and they consumed the two Testaments. For this reason the prophet David said, "like the deaf asp that stops her ears; which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charmed cunningly by a skilled one." The Jews are called the asp; for they stopped up their ears, who would not hearken to the voice of the charmers, that is, of the Bridegroom, nor to the harmonies of the divine Scriptures. The devil too is called the asp, the opposing powers are called its fierce heats, the threshing-floor place is Hades, the hole is the storehouse of Hades. Who is the charmer? Christ. What are the seven handfuls? The seven ages. What is the staff of twelve cubits? The twelve-stringed lyre of David. What is the charming? The voice of the Saviour, who said, "Come, Adam, thou who wast once my sheep," and drove away the devil, and conquered the whole hollow of Hades.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the asp.

div.head: Concerning the Swallow
div.p: The swallow is a devoted bird [and swift of flight]. It travels half its time in the wilderness, and half in the open country, [that is, near men], bearing young [both in the wilderness and in the open country, and making its nest in the houses of men]. And when they have made their young, [they both travel, and bring food, and nourish them; and] often one of them is blinded, and at once the female travels into the wilderness, and brings back an herb, and lays it upon the eyes of the blinded one, and at once it is healed and sees again.

And so you too, understanding man, according to what the Prophet says, "I have lodged in the wilderness," walk in this way, that both in this present age and in the age to come you may have fruit [unto the forgiveness of sins]; and when you fall into sins and your understanding is blinded, go into the wilderness, that is, into a city of refuge, and take the herb, that is, repentance, and lay it upon the blindness of your impiety, and, for the sake of the consubstantial Trinity, the blindness of sin shall be rooted out of you.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the swallow.

div.head: Concerning the Woodpecker
div.p: The woodpecker is a bird of many colours, just as the devil too is of many colours. This same woodpecker enters into the woodland thicket, and climbs up the trees, and taps with its beak, and listens with its ear, and if the tree is hollow and without heartwood, it makes a cutting, and enters into it, and nests, [and breeds its young]; but if the tree is sound, [cheerful] and whole of heart, it quickly withdraws from it, and goes to another.

So too the devil [travels in the thicket, that is, in human nature, and] climbs upon the trees, that is, upon men, tapping with the arrows of uncleanness, and listens with his ear, and if the man is hollow and without heart, [at once] he enters into him and nests [in his heart]; but if the man is sound and whole of heart, he withdraws from him quickly, and goes into another thicket.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the woodpecker.

div.head: Concerning the Hoopoe
div.p: The hoopoe is a bird more devoted to its father and more devoted to its mother than all the birds [of the sky]. Know, understanding man, even though it is a small bird, what wisdom God has given it, and how it cherishes its parents. The male and the female travel together, and make their young in the hollows of trees, [and they both travel,] and bring food, and nourish their young, and when their young are grown, the parents shed their feathers, and become as fledglings themselves, [and sit in the nest,] unable to fly [and bring themselves food, and be nourished]. How then shall they live? Listen: the young go forth [and take counsel] with good counsel; ["since our parents raised us with toil and pain, and brought us to maturity, let us also go"], and they bring food, and nourish their parents, and make up to them the toil owed in return.

And so you too, understanding man, know that you were born of father and mother, and that with toil and pain and groaning they raised you, and brought you to full manhood; go, then, you too, and render recompense and service in return to your parents [until their old age and the end of their life], that the blessing of father and mother may come upon you, supporting you against every wickedness, and become an imitator of that bird.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the hoopoe.

div.head: Concerning the Fox
div.p: The fox is a creature of many turns beyond all creatures. And when it hungers [for food] and finds nothing to eat, in what manner does it act? Listen: it goes to a sunny place, and lays itself upon the ground, [and stretches out,] and holds its breath [until it swells up], and its body is stiffened as though dead, [and it lies on its back, with its eyes and feet upward]. Then the birds of the sky come, wishing to devour it, and it rises up suddenly, and hunts them, [and eats as many as it wishes].
So too the devil, when he wishes to ensnare a man, in order to tempt him the more, even helps him on his way, so that he neglects prayer, and easily ensnares him.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the fox.

div.head: Concerning the Viper
div.p: The viper has, from the middle upward, the form of a man, and from the middle downward, the form of a crocodile. [The female has no organs, but the male alone has organs, as with the asp also.] The male and the female travel together, and when the female is inflamed, [she goes up to the male, and] devours the necessary parts of the male, and conceives, and the male dies at once; and when the days draw near for the female to give birth, since she has no other means, her young gnaw through the belly of their mother, and so come forth, [for she has no other nature, and the mother too dies at once, and] they come forth thereafter as slayers of father and mother.

just as the Jews too became slayers of father and mother: they killed the father, that is, Christ, they killed the mother, that is, the Church. For this reason John also reproached them, saying, "O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?"
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the viper.

div.head: Concerning the Gorgon
div.p: The gorgon has the shape of a [beautiful] harlot woman; the hairs of her head are as it were serpents, and the look of her face is death. She sports and laughs only at the time [of her desire], and she grazes among the mountains of the west, and when the day of her desire arrives, she begins to cry out, from the lion and the rest of the animals down to man, to beast, to bird, and to dragon, saying, "Come to me, [all of you,] and enjoy carnal desire"; and thereupon [all] that hear her voice go to her, and, seeing her, at once they die. For she knows all the tongues of animals, both of men and of beasts. And in what manner does the charmer master her? Listen: he knows, through astronomy, the day of her desire, and goes toward the place of her dwelling, charming from afar; and she begins to cry out from the lion first, and the rest of the animals, and when she comes to the tongue of the charmer, the charmer answers her, saying, ["I cannot see thee, but] dig for thyself a pit in an upper place, and put thy head there, that I may not see thee and die, and that I may come and lie with thee"; and she, hearing this, does so at once. Then the charmer approaches from behind [with a drawn sword], and beheads her, and does not look upon her head, lest he die, but [covers his face, and goes off, and] casts it into a vessel, [and binds it securely]; and whatever dragon or other beast he sees, [or man his enemy, with skill,] he shows [it] the head of the gorgon, and dries it up, just as also Alexander the king possessed it, and [by means of it] mastered all the nations.
And so you too, understanding man, having your mind of one accord with God, shall easily master the opposing powers.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the gorgon.

div.head: Concerning the Serpent
div.p: For he said through the holy Apostle, "be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves." And in what is it wise as a serpent, and what is the nature of the serpent?

The serpent has three natures in itself, and its first nature is this: when it grows old, its eyes grow dim, and it does not see, and, [feeling its way,] it enters into a narrow crack of the rock, and fasts forty days [and forty nights], and humbles itself, [and comes out through a narrower hole,] and sheds its old garment, and becomes young again.

And so you too, understanding man, having fasted forty days [and forty nights, humble yourself, and] cast off your old garment, that is, the old deception of the devil, and [thus] put on the new man that is being renewed, that is, Christ.

And the second nature of the serpent is this: when it goes to the water to drink, it lays aside its poison in its lair, and so goes forth clean [and drinks], lest it poison those who drink of it after, [or destroy itself].

And so you too, understanding man, going in the pure and undefiled Church of Christ, lay aside every wickedness and slander [and blasphemy] and evil thought [that you have in your heart] in your house, and so go forth clean and undefiled [into the Church of Christ], that you may not poison [your soul, but receive purely] the holy body and precious blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.
And the third nature of the serpent is this: when it sees a man naked, it flees from him, but when it sees him clothed, it enters upon him and makes war on him.

So too the devil, if he sees a man stripped of the corruptible garment [and clothed in faith], flees from him; but if he sees him [stripped of faith and] clothed in the corruptible garment, he enters upon him and makes war on him.
[The fourth nature of the serpent: when the serpent is again warred upon by man, it gives up its whole body to blows, but covers its head on every side with the whole of its body.]

[When you see the devil making war on you, do not listen to him and be mastered by him, but make war against him in return, and keep your chastity spotless and undefiled, and your faith, as the serpent keeps its head, and so you shall not be mastered by him.]
For this reason the Lord said, "be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves." Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the serpent.

div.head: Concerning the Hare
div.p: The hare is a runner in that it flees swiftly, and when it flees the hunter, if it makes for the high ridges, the dogs together with the hunter grow weary, and are not able to hunt it down; but if it makes for the depths, it is quickly caught.

And so you too, understanding man, if you make for the heights [the mountains, of which David also said, "I have lifted up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help"], that is, the virtues and the ways of life inspired by God, the opposing powers together with the hunter, that is, the devil, grow weary, and you are not overtaken; but if you give yourself to the depths, that is, to error and sin, you are overtaken by the opposing powers.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the hare.

div.head: Concerning the Frog, the Dry (also called Sakkos) and the Wet
div.p: This dry frog receives the burning heat of the sun, and the frosts and rains and winds and storms, and endures all things, and grows weary in no way; but the wet frog is able to bear none of these things, but when winter comes, it casts itself into the depths, and when the sun shines, it comes forth and warms itself pleasantly, and when the heat of the sun grows thick upon it, being unable to bear it, it casts itself again into the depths, [and this same wet frog will not be able to bear anything excessive].

So too the monks who take up the ascetic life will be able to endure all things: hunger, thirst, nakedness, self-restraint and lying on the bare ground, [want of washing, dry food, insult, mourning, tears, freedom from passion,] and will be burdened by nothing; but the worldly will be able to bear none of these things, and will not even begin to fast gladly, but without delay will draw ever nearer to gluttony.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the frog.

div.head: Concerning the Ant
div.p: The ant is small among creeping things, yet its works are greatest. Know then, you too, O man, how it labours: when the season of the harvest arrives, they clear their threshing-path and their road, and go into the fields [and to the threshing-floors], and if it is barley, they pass by it, going instead to the wheat; for since the barley's husks are strong, they cannot fully take hold of its grains, but since the wheat's husks are loose, they take hold of its grains easily, and carry them up to their threshing-place. And when they are filled [with rain], in what manner do they treat the grains, that they may not sprout and be lost to them as food? They cut the grain through the middle, and pare it thin, lest [winter come and] it sprout, [and they themselves die].

So too the opposing powers go forth into the fields, that is, among mortal men, and go up into the ears of corn, that is, into the hearts of men, and if it is barley, that is, one having a hard heart, they withdraw from him; but if it is wheat, that is, one having a loose heart, they take the grain from him, that is, his faith, and carry it up to the threshing-floor, that is, to perdition, and they cut it and pare it thin, that the Holy Spirit may no longer sprout in it, but that they may perish together with it.
Well has the Physiologus spoken concerning the ant.
